questions.q: a) List out the methods involved in memory management. [L1][CO6] [2M]
questions.a: The main memory-management methods are: (1) contiguous allocation — single-partition and multiple-partition schemes using fixed or variable (dynamic) partitions; (2) non-contiguous allocation — paging and segmentation, and their combination segmented paging; (3) swapping, in which a whole process is rolled out to a backing store and back in; and (4) virtual memory techniques — demand paging and demand segmentation. These methods are often combined, for example paging with swapping and demand paging. Each method aims to maximize memory utilization and the number of resident processes while providing isolation and protection.
questions.explanation: This lists the standard taxonomy of memory-management schemes from simple contiguous allocation through paging/segmentation to virtual memory and swapping.
questions.oneShotPreview: Methods: contiguous (fixed/variable partitions), paging, segmentation, swapping, demand paging/virtual memory.

questions.q: b) Describe virtual memory with neat diagram. [L1][CO6] [2M]
questions.a: Virtual memory is a technique that allows a process to execute even when it is not entirely resident in main memory: its logical (virtual) address space is mapped to physical memory by the memory-management unit (MMU), and only the currently needed pages are kept in RAM while the rest stay on a disk backing (swap) area. In a typical diagram the CPU sends a logical address (page number + offset) to the MMU, which consults the page table to obtain the frame number and access physical memory; a miss triggers demand paging that transfers the page from the swap area on disk into a free frame. This separation of logical and physical memory lets more processes run concurrently, frees programs from physical-memory limits and contiguity requirements, and enables sharing and protection. The OS maintains the page table with valid/invalid bits to distinguish resident pages from those on disk.
questions.explanation: The answer explains the logical-to-physical mapping, the backing store and demand paging, and the benefits shown in the conventional CPU → MMU → memory/disk diagram.
questions.oneShotPreview: Virtual memory = logical addresses mapped by MMU/page table to RAM frames; non-resident pages fetched from disk on demand.

questions.q: c) What is meant by Paging and Page fault? [L1][CO6] [2M]
questions.a: Paging is a non-contiguous memory-management scheme in which physical memory is split into fixed-size blocks called frames and a process's logical address space into equal-size blocks called pages; a page table maps each logical page to a physical frame, so a page may be placed anywhere in RAM and external fragmentation is eliminated. A page fault is an exception raised by the MMU when a process references a page whose page-table entry is marked invalid (the page is not in main memory). The OS services it by locating the page on the backing store, obtaining a free frame (evicting a victim page if needed), loading the page, updating the page table and TLB, and then restarting the faulting instruction.
questions.explanation: This defines both terms precisely and connects them: paging supplies the page/frame mapping, and a page fault is the trap that implements demand paging when a mapped page is absent.
questions.oneShotPreview: Paging: fixed-size pages → frames via page table. Page fault: trap when referenced page is not in RAM; OS loads it.

questions.q: d) Discuss Belady’s Anomaly phenomenon in OS. [L1][CO6] [2M]
questions.a: Belady's anomaly is the counter-intuitive situation in which, for certain reference strings, allocating more page frames results in more page faults instead of fewer. It is exhibited by FIFO (and other non-stack) replacement algorithms, which do not guarantee that the set of pages resident with n frames is a subset of the set resident with n+1 frames. A classic example is the string 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5: FIFO produces 9 faults with three frames but 10 faults with four frames. Stack algorithms such as LRU and Optimal never show this anomaly, which is why they are preferred. The anomaly arises because a recently used page can be evicted early under FIFO even though extra frames were available.
questions.explanation: The definition, the stack-property explanation, and a concrete counterexample fully account for the phenomenon and why it matters.
questions.oneShotPreview: Belady: more frames → more faults under FIFO (e.g. 9 faults/3 frames vs 10/4); LRU & Optimal never show it.

questions.q: e) What is Seek time and Rotational Latency? [L1][CO6] [2M]
questions.a: Seek time is the time required for the disk arm/actuator to move the read-write head from its current track to the track containing the requested block; it is usually the dominant part of a disk access. Rotational latency (rotational delay) is the additional time the platter must spin until the desired sector rotates under the head, averaging half a revolution. Together with transfer time and queuing delay, these components determine the total access time to a disk block. Disk-scheduling algorithms such as SSTF, SCAN and C-SCAN mainly try to reduce seek time, while placing related blocks close together reduces rotational latency.
questions.explanation: This distinguishes head movement time from platter rotation time, the two principal mechanical delays in magnetic-disk access.
questions.oneShotPreview: Seek time = arm moves to target track; rotational latency = wait for sector to spin under head (avg ½ revolution).

questions.q: 2 a) What is memory management? List and discuss about various techniques of managing memory in operating systems. [L2][CO6] [5M]
questions.a: Memory management is the OS function of allocating main memory to processes, tracking what is resident, protecting one process's area from another, and reclaiming memory when it is no longer needed. Its techniques include: contiguous allocation, where each process gets one block (single partition, fixed partitions/MFT, or variable partitions/MVT with first-fit, best-fit or worst-fit); paging, which divides memory into fixed-size frames and a process into pages mapped by a page table; segmentation, which divides a program into logical variable-size segments with base and limit registers; segmented paging, a combination of both; swapping, which moves whole processes between memory and backing store; and virtual memory with demand paging, which loads only the pages currently required. Contiguous schemes are simple but fragment memory, while paging and segmentation remove external fragmentation and, with demand paging, allow processes larger than physical memory.
questions.explanation: The answer defines the function, enumerates the recognized techniques, and discusses their distinguishing behavior and trade-offs, as expected for a 5-mark question.
questions.oneShotPreview: Memory management = allocate, track, protect, reclaim RAM; techniques: contiguous, paging, segmentation, swapping, virtual memory.

questions.q: b) Explain about contiguous memory allocation in detail [L2][CO6] [5M]
questions.a: Contiguous memory allocation assigns each process a single continuous block of main memory. In the simplest single-partition scheme, the OS occupies one part of memory and the single user process occupies the rest. In fixed-partition allocation (MFT), memory is divided into a set of fixed-size partitions, each holding one process — simple, but an oversized program cannot fit and small jobs waste space through internal fragmentation. In variable-partition allocation (MVT), the OS maintains a list of available holes and allocates a hole of the right size using first-fit, best-fit or worst-fit, which leads to external fragmentation as holes accumulate between processes. Protection is provided by base and limit (relocation/limit) registers that check every address, and fragmentation can be reduced by compaction, which shifts processes together to create one large free block (requiring dynamic relocation).
questions.explanation: It covers the single-partition, fixed-partition and variable-partition variants, allocation strategies, fragmentation types, protection registers and compaction — the standard detail for this topic.
questions.oneShotPreview: Contiguous allocation: one block per process; fixed vs variable partitions, first/best/worst-fit, internal & external fragmentation, base/limit registers, compaction.

questions.q: 3 What is paging in operating systems, and how does it help manage memory efficiently? Give example. [L2][CO6] [10M]
questions.a: Paging is a non-contiguous memory-management scheme that divides physical memory into fixed-size blocks called frames and a process's logical address space into blocks of the same size called pages; a page table maintained by the OS maps each logical page number to a physical frame number, while the offset within the page is unchanged. A logical address generated by the CPU is split into a page number p (used as an index into the page table) and an offset d (added to the frame base address) to form the physical address. Because pages may be placed in any free frame, paging eliminates external fragmentation and the need for a process to occupy contiguous memory; it also makes sharing of code and protection bits per page straightforward, and it is the basis of demand paging and virtual memory. For example, with a 32-bit address space and 4 KB (2^12 byte) pages, an address is divided into a 20-bit page number and a 12-bit offset, giving 2^20 (about one million) pages; if page 4 of a process is mapped to frame 9, then logical address (4, offset 100) maps to physical address 9×4096 + 100. The cost is internal fragmentation of at most one partial page per process and the memory needed for page tables, which is why TLBs and multilevel tables are used.
questions.explanation: This gives the definition, address-translation mechanism, efficiency benefits, a concrete numeric example and the trade-offs — the breadth required for a 10-mark answer.
questions.oneShotPreview: Paging maps equal-size logical pages to physical frames via a page table; removes external fragmentation, enables virtual memory. Example: 32-bit, 4 KB pages → 20-bit page + 12-bit offset.

questions.q: 4 Explain the different techniques used to structure page tables in operating systems, and how do they help manage large address spaces efficiently? [L2][CO6] [10M]
questions.a: A simple flat page table maps every virtual page to a frame in one table, but a 32-bit space with 4 KB pages would need about 2^20 entries per process — far too much memory to keep contiguous. Hierarchical (multilevel) page tables solve this by dividing the page number into levels: the first-level table indexes second-level tables, and unused portions of the address space need no lower-level tables, so only the tables for actually used regions are allocated. For a 64-bit space, four or more levels are used; each level adds a memory access, but a translation lookaside buffer (TLB) caches recent translations so most lookups need no table walk. An inverted page table keeps one entry per physical frame (number of frames, not virtual pages), storing the process id and virtual page for each frame; it is compact but makes sharing harder and lookup slower, so it is often combined with a hash table. Hashed page tables use a hash of the virtual page number with chaining to handle collisions, which is efficient for sparse, large address spaces. Combining these structures with a TLB makes virtual memory practical: memory use for tables stays proportional to physical memory or to allocated regions rather than to the entire virtual space.
questions.explanation: It covers hierarchical, inverted and hashed page tables plus the TLB and explicitly explains how each reduces table memory for large address spaces.
questions.oneShotPreview: Page-table structures: multilevel/hierarchical, inverted, hashed + TLB caching — reduce table size for huge virtual address spaces.

questions.q: 5 a) Describe about Swapping in memory management with its advantage and disadvantages. [L2][CO6] [5M]
questions.a: Swapping is a memory-management technique in which a process that is blocked or needs memory is moved (rolled out) from main memory to a backing store such as a disk swap area, and later brought back (rolled in) when it is ready to run again. A swap-out frees the memory it occupied for another process, and a swap-out/swap-in pair is triggered by the scheduler when memory is overcommitted or a higher-priority process needs space. Advantages include allowing more processes to be resident than physical memory can hold, supporting multiprogramming with limited RAM, and giving better response by suspending inactive processes. Disadvantages are the high disk I/O cost and transfer time, which can severely degrade performance when swapping is frequent; only whole processes can be swapped in simple schemes, and context/state must be saved and restored. Swapping is often combined with demand paging, where individual pages rather than whole processes are moved.
questions.explanation: The answer defines roll-out/roll-in, gives the mechanism and context, and lists balanced advantages and disadvantages as the question requests.
questions.oneShotPreview: Swapping = move idle processes to disk and back. Pros: more resident processes; cons: slow disk I/O, overhead.

questions.q: b) Analyze the difference between Paging and Segmentation. [L4][CO6] [5M]
questions.a: Paging divides both physical memory and a process's logical address space into fixed-size blocks (frames and pages, typically 4 KB) managed by a page table, chosen by the OS for efficient memory use; the user is unaware of the division. Segmentation divides a program into variable-size logical units such as code, data, stack and heap, each with a base and a limit, managed by a segment table; segments are visible to the programmer and correspond to meaningful program units. Paging suffers only internal fragmentation (up to one partial page per segment) and no external fragmentation, whereas segmentation suffers external fragmentation because segments vary in size but has no internal fragmentation. Paging therefore supports virtual memory and simple allocation well, while segmentation better supports sharing, protection, and dynamic data structures. A segmented-paging system combines both to gain the logical structure of segments and the allocation efficiency of pages.
questions.explanation: The comparison covers unit size, table used, fragmentation behavior, visibility to the programmer, and sharing/protection trade-offs — the dimensions expected in an analysis question.
questions.oneShotPreview: Paging: fixed-size pages/frames, page table, internal fragmentation. Segmentation: variable logical segments, segment table, external fragmentation.

questions.q: 6 Discuss segmentation in operating system with an example. [L2][CO6] [10M]
questions.a: Segmentation is a non-contiguous memory-management scheme in which a program is divided into several variable-length logical segments, typically main code, data, stack and heap, rather than into uniform pages. Each segment has a base address (its starting physical location) and a limit (its length), stored in a segment table; a logical address consists of a segment number and an offset, and the hardware checks that the offset is less than the limit before adding it to the base to form the physical address. This makes sharing and protection natural — a code segment can be marked read-only and shared by several processes while data segments remain private — and it matches the programmer's view of a program. For example, if the code segment (number 0) has base 1000 and limit 500, then logical address (0, 120) maps to physical address 1120, while (0, 600) is trapped as an addressing error. Because segments are allocated dynamically, segmentation creates external fragmentation (holes between segments) which may require compaction; combining segmentation with paging (segmented paging) avoids this by paging each segment. Segmentation can also be combined with demand loading (demand segmentation) to support virtual memory.
questions.explanation: It explains the segment table with base/limit, the logical-address format, sharing and protection benefits, a worked example, and the fragmentation drawback plus the segmented-paging remedy — appropriate depth for 10 marks.
questions.oneShotPreview: Segmentation: variable-size code/data/stack segments with base+limit and offset checks; enables sharing/protection but causes external fragmentation.

questions.q: 7 Illustrate the procedure for page fault in demand paging with neat diagram. [L3][CO6] [10M]
questions.a: In demand paging a page is loaded into memory only when it is first referenced; if the page is not resident, the MMU raises a page-fault trap. The procedure is: (1) the CPU generates a logical address and the MMU checks the page-table entry; if the valid/invalid bit is invalid, a page fault traps to the OS. (2) The OS saves the current process context (registers, program counter) and checks that the reference is legal; if it is invalid it terminates the process, otherwise it continues. (3) The OS finds a free frame in main memory; if none is free it runs a page-replacement algorithm (FIFO, LRU, Optimal, etc.) to select a victim frame, writes the victim out to disk if it was modified (using the dirty bit). (4) It issues a disk read to bring the required page from the backing store into the free frame. (5) It updates the page table (and invalidates/updates the TLB) so the entry maps to the new frame and marks it valid. (6) It restores the saved context and restarts the instruction that caused the fault, so the memory reference now succeeds transparently. A typical diagram shows CPU → MMU/page table → physical memory, with an arrow from the page fault handler to the swap area on disk and back. Effective access time is EAT = (1 − p) × memory access time + p × page-fault service time, so a low fault rate p is essential.
questions.explanation: This gives the complete, correctly ordered fault-handling sequence, the role of the valid/dirty bits and replacement algorithm, a diagram description, and the EAT relationship.
questions.oneShotPreview: Page fault: invalid PTE → trap → save context → find/evict frame → read page from disk → update PTE/TLB → restart instruction.

questions.q: 8 a) Describe in detail about CoW technique [L2][CO6] [5M]
questions.a: Copy-on-Write (CoW) is an optimization used when a page might be shared by two or more processes, most famously during fork(). Instead of immediately duplicating the parent's pages, the parent and child initially share the same physical frames, and both page-table entries are marked read-only with a CoW flag. As long as neither process writes, no copy is made, saving memory and time. When either process writes to a shared page, the MMU raises a protection fault; the OS checks the CoW flag, allocates a new frame, copies the page contents into it, updates the writing process's page-table entry to point to the private copy with write permission, and restarts the instruction, leaving the other process with the original page. CoW therefore makes process creation fast and memory-efficient by deferring copying until it is actually needed, while still preserving process isolation; it is also used by file systems, snapshotting and memory-mapping facilities.
questions.explanation: It explains the shared read-only pages, fault-triggered duplication, and the resulting benefit, which is the complete mechanism of copy-on-write.
questions.oneShotPreview: CoW: fork shares frames read-only; first write faults, copies the page, gives writer a private frame — fast, memory-saving.

questions.q: b) Consider the following reference string 7,0,1,2,0,3,0,4,2,3,0,3,2,1,2,0,1,7,0,1. Assume there are three frames. Apply LRU replacement algorithm to the reference sting above and find out how many page faults are produced. Illustrate the LRU page replacement algorithm in detail. [L3][CO6] [5M]
questions.a: LRU (Least Recently Used) replaces the page that has not been referenced for the longest time, using recent past access as a prediction of future behavior; it can be implemented with counters or a stack and is a stack algorithm, so it never suffers Belady's anomaly. Simulating the string with three initially empty frames: 7(F) → [7]; 0(F) → [7,0]; 1(F) → [7,0,1]; 2(F, evict 7) → [0,1,2]; 0(hit) → [1,2,0]; 3(F, evict 1) → [2,0,3]; 0(hit) → [2,3,0]; 4(F, evict 2) → [3,0,4]; 2(F, evict 3) → [0,4,2]; 3(F, evict 0) → [4,2,3]; 0(F, evict 4) → [2,3,0]; 3(hit) → [2,0,3]; 2(hit) → [0,3,2]; 1(F, evict 0) → [3,2,1]; 2(hit) → [3,1,2]; 0(F, evict 3) → [1,2,0]; 1(hit) → [2,0,1]; 7(F, evict 2) → [0,1,7]; 0(hit) → [1,7,0]; 1(hit) → [7,0,1]. The three initial references are compulsory (cold) faults, and subsequent faults occur when a needed page is absent and the least recently used page is evicted. Total page faults = 12 (8 hits out of 20 references), giving a fault rate of 60%.
questions.explanation: The frame-by-frame trace shows every hit, fault and victim, so the count of 12 is reproducible; the implementation and stack-property notes cover the 'illustrate in detail' part.

questions.q: 9 Given page reference string: 1,2,3,2,1,5,2,1,6,2,5,6,3,1,3,6,1,2,4,3. Compare the number of page faults for LRU, FIFO and Optimal page replacement algorithm. [L4][CO6] [10M]
questions.a: Assuming three page frames (the standard assumption for this problem), simulate each policy on the 20-reference string. FIFO replaces the oldest page regardless of use: faults occur at references 1,2,3,5,8,9,10,11,13,14,16,18,19,20, giving 14 page faults. LRU replaces the least recently used page: faults at 1,2,3,6,9,11,13,14,18,19,20, giving 11 page faults. Optimal (MIN) replaces the page whose next use is farthest in the future (or never): faults at 1,2,3,6,9,13,14,18,19, giving 9 page faults. Thus Optimal < LRU < FIFO in fault count, confirming that Optimal is the theoretical lower bound, LRU approximates it well, and FIFO is weakest (and can even exhibit Belady's anomaly). LRU and Optimal are stack algorithms, so increasing frames never increases their faults, while FIFO is not. If a different frame count is assumed the exact numbers change, but the ordering Optimal ≤ LRU ≤ FIFO generally holds.
questions.explanation: The answer states the frame assumption, gives all three fault counts, explains each policy's victim choice, and draws the correct comparison that Optimal is best and FIFO worst.
questions.oneShotPreview: 3 frames: FIFO = 14 faults, LRU = 11 faults, Optimal = 9 faults — Optimal best, FIFO worst.

questions.q: 10 a) Discuss about frame allocation and the algorithms used to achieve it. [L2][CO6] [5M]
questions.a: Frame allocation decides how many physical frames each process receives when demand paging is used. The minimum number of frames a process needs is determined by its instruction set (e.g., a machine that needs up to N operands per instruction must have at least N frames), while the maximum is the number of frames in physical memory. The equal-allocation strategy splits m frames among n processes (m/n each, with leftovers distributed), which is simple but ignores process size. Proportional allocation gives frames in proportion to each process's size, so larger processes get more frames. Priority allocation reserves extra frames for high-priority processes, sometimes taking them from lower-priority ones. Replacement can be global, where any process's frame may be chosen as victim, or local, where a process can only replace its own frames; local replacement gives more predictable per-process performance. The working-set model and the page-fault frequency (PFF) algorithm are used to tune allocation dynamically: increase frames when the fault rate is high and decrease it when it is low, which also helps prevent thrashing.
questions.explanation: It defines minimum/maximum frame needs and covers equal, proportional, priority, global vs local allocation plus working-set/PFF tuning — the complete set of allocation algorithms.
questions.oneShotPreview: Frame allocation: equal, proportional, priority; global vs local replacement; working set & PFF tune frames to avoid thrashing.

questions.q: b) What is thrashing? Explain the causes of thrashing in detail. [L2][CO6] [5M]
questions.a: Thrashing is a condition in which a process spends more time swapping pages in and out than executing useful instructions, causing a severe drop in CPU utilization and system throughput. It happens when the total number of frames demanded by the active processes exceeds the available physical memory, so each process lacks the frames needed to hold its working set (the set of pages it actively uses in a locality). A page fault frees a frame that is then immediately needed by another process, producing a chain of continuous page faults and disk I/O; the CPU sits idle while the disk is saturated. Causes include over-committing memory by admitting too many processes, poor locality or a program jumping between many pages, bad replacement choices, and global replacement that lets one process take frames from others. Remedies include local or priority-based replacement, working-set and page-fault-frequency algorithms to adjust each process's frame allocation, suspending some processes (swap out) to reduce the degree of multiprogramming, and providing more physical memory.
questions.explanation: It defines thrashing, explains the working-set and paging-storm mechanism, lists its causes and gives standard remedies, which is the expected detailed treatment.
questions.oneShotPreview: Thrashing = constant paging, little execution; caused by too many processes/small working sets; fix via working-set/PFF, local replacement, lower multiprogramming.

questions.q: 11 a) Describe Mass Storage Structure Devices. [L2][CO6] [5M]
questions.a: Mass-storage devices are secondary-storage media used to store large amounts of data persistently. Magnetic disks (hard disks) consist of one or more rotating platters coated with magnetic material; data is recorded in concentric tracks divided into sectors, and tracks at the same radius on all platters form a cylinder; a read-write head on a movable arm accesses a sector after seeking to its track and waiting for rotation. Access time is the sum of seek time, rotational latency and transfer time. Solid-state drives (SSDs) use flash memory with no moving parts, giving much faster random access and lower latency but higher cost per bit and limited write endurance. Optical disks (CD, DVD, Blu-ray) store data on a reflective track read by a laser and are mainly used for distribution and archival. Magnetic tape stores data sequentially on a moving ribbon; it is slow for random access but cheap and suitable for backups and archives. These devices differ in capacity, speed, cost and access pattern, and form the storage hierarchy below main memory.
questions.explanation: It describes the principal mass-storage device types, the magnetic-disk geometry and access-time components, and their relative trade-offs.
questions.oneShotPreview: Mass storage: magnetic disks (tracks/sectors/cylinders; seek+rotation+transfer), SSDs (flash, no moving parts), optical disks, tapes.

questions.q: b) Explain in detail about Disk management. [L2][CO6] [5M]
questions.a: Disk management is the set of OS activities that make a raw disk usable for storing files. It begins with low-level (physical) formatting, which divides each track into sectors and writes the header/trailer information and error-correcting codes the controller needs. The disk is then partitioned into independent logical volumes, and each partition may be high-level formatted with a file system that records its metadata (including a boot block containing the bootstrap loader used at startup). The OS keeps track of free space with a free-space list implemented as a bitmap or a linked list of free blocks, allocating and reclaiming blocks as files are created and deleted. Bad blocks are detected and either marked unusable or remapped to spare sectors by the controller. Disk-scheduling algorithms (FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK, C-LOOK) decide the order of I/O requests to minimize seek time, and RAID (redundant arrays of independent disks) combines multiple disks with mirroring, parity and striping to improve performance and reliability. The OS also handles disk I/O through device drivers with buffering and caching and may provide disk quotas and defragmentation.
questions.explanation: It covers the full lifecycle — formatting, partitioning, boot blocks, free-space management, bad-block handling, scheduling and RAID — which is what a detailed disk-management answer requires.
questions.oneShotPreview: Disk management: physical format → partitioning → file system/boot block → free-space list → bad blocks → disk scheduling/RAID → quotas.
